scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Calabrian tarantella traces its roots to ancient Greek dance traditions, characterized by upright postures, a waist-level center of gravity, and expressive freedom rather than rigid codification.
Unlike the tarantellas of Naples or the Apulian phenomenon of tarantism, it evolved as a festive and religious-processional expression with deep cultural roots.
Traditional instruments like the ancient aulos and tympanon eventually gave way to the zampogna, organetto, and tamburello.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The rota symbolizes the community's territory, with the dance representing the conquest and sharing of that space.
Same-sex dances symbolize a duel for territorial dominance, while mixed-gender dances enact traditional courtship rituals characterized by female modesty and male displays of agility.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performed by couples—man-woman, man-man, or woman-woman—within a circular community space called a rota.
The master of dance (u mastru i ballu) manages turns and selects participants.
Movement features an upright, static trunk combined with frantic lower-body footwork based on terzine.
Watch for Soprappasso (Intricciata), Tagghjapassu, Illi adornu.

Formation: Couples dance counter-clockwise inside a single circular space called a rota.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is driven by terzine rhythms in 12/8 and sometimes 6/8 time.
Primary instruments include the zampogna (bagpipe) and its common modern replacement the organetto (diatonic accordion), accompanied by the tamburello (frame drum).
Listen for the zampogna, organetto, tamburello, pipita.
The pulse is 12/8 and 6/8 time.
Driven by terzine rhythms in 12/8 or 6/8 time, featuring the reedy drone of the zampogna or organetto underpinned by the sharp acoustic pulse of the tamburello.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditionally danced in public piazze during religious festivals and community celebrations.
Dancers utilize everyday festive attire, with women frequently incorporating a foulard as a choreographic prop and challenge symbol.
In Vibonese, the 6/8 rhythm of the tarantella traditionally accompanies the dance of the Giganti—enormous papier-mâché figures operated from within by dancers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The tradition is anchored by community elders, traditional musicians playing 'ad usu anticu', and the u mastru i ballu (master of dance) who arbitrates social dynamics and manages turn-taking within the rota.
Geographical variants include the libera in east Catanzarese, the sonu a ballu in Aspromonte, the zumparieddu in Sila, and the viddanedda in Reggio Calabria.
A distinct branch of southern Italian tarantella descending from ancient Greek choreographic forms, entirely separate from Neapolitan tarantella and tarantism rituals.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Calabrian tarantella is parent of tarantella: Broad category of southern Italian dances from which Calabrian tarantella is distinguished by rhythm and form.
Calabrian tarantella is influence of ballu sardu: Shares uncodified traditional Greek-derived spatial and bodily movement characteristics.
Calabrian tarantella is influence of sirtaki: Shares ancient Greek dance roots emphasizing earth contact and community circle formations.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright posture with the center of gravity positioned at the waist and a static trunk.
Men elevate and move arms expansively (miming knife fights in male pairings); women keep arms below shoulder height or resting on hips with palms outward.
Independent movement from the waist down, while the trunk remains static.
